redditSourcedNotes: VERIFY STAGE (2026-09-11). The researcher's 12 draft queries never executed (search budget was exhausted), so the draft was built from model knowledge with no sources. The verify stage had 5 searches and spent them on the highest-doubt items: (1) Accents Coffee & Tea Lounge announced permanent closure in July 2020 (lovindublin.com, her.ie) and was DROPPED; (2) Books Upstairs is confirmed open at 17 D'Olier Street with a first-floor cafe (booksupstairs.ie, dublincityofliterature.ie) but has no English Wikipedia article of its own, so its wikipediaTitle is null; (3) St Kevin's Park is a Dublin City Council park (dublincity.ie) and the Wikipedia article 'St. Kevin's Church, Camden Row, Dublin' is about the ruined church inside it, so that title is used; (4) 'Blessington Street Basin' and (5) 'Sandymount Strand' Wikipedia titles confirmed from result URLs. The remaining Wikipedia titles (Iveagh Gardens, Chester Beatty Library, National Library of Ireland, Poolbeg Lighthouse, North Bull Island, National Botanic Gardens (Ireland), Killiney Hill) are well-known landmark articles kept on reviewer knowledge without a search. No reddit thread was read in either stage, so no spot is reddit-sourced; sources listed are the official, press and blog pages that actually appeared in the verify searches. Hours are approximate and should be re-checked seasonally.

spots.name: Iveagh Gardens
spots.blurb: A walled Victorian garden tucked behind the National Concert Hall that many people walk straight past on Harcourt Street. Inside are a rustic cascade, a sunken lawn, a rosarium and a small yew maze, with far fewer people than St Stephen's Green two minutes away. Bring a book and a sandwich and take a bench under the trees near the fountains.
spots.tips: Enter from Clonmel Street (off Harcourt Street) or through the gate behind the Concert Hall on Earlsfort Terrace; gates lock at closing so check the sign on the way in. Quietest on weekday mornings, fills up on sunny lunchtimes.
spots.hours: approx 8am-6pm summer, till 4pm winter (Sun from 10am); check OPW site

safety.note: Enclosed OPW park with staff on site; daytime only as the gates are locked at closing.

spots.name: Blessington Street Basin
spots.blurb: A former city reservoir (1810 to the 1970s) turned walled pond-garden in Phibsborough, ringed by a gravel path, mature trees and benches, with ducks, moorhens, swans and the odd heron. It is enclosed and quiet and feels a long way from Dorset Street traffic. Sit at the far end opposite the little island and let an hour go.
spots.tips: The gate is at the top of Blessington Street; the park is locked at dusk so it is a daytime spot. Weekday afternoons are almost empty.
spots.hours: approx 8am-dusk (varies seasonally); check Dublin City Council site

spots.name: Chester Beatty
spots.blurb: A free museum of manuscripts and art from Asia, the Middle East and Europe, set in the gardens behind Dublin Castle. The upstairs galleries are hushed and low-lit, the Silk Road Cafe does good food, and in fair weather the small roof garden is one of the calmest places to sit in the city centre. On rainy days it is the obvious refuge.
spots.tips: Enter through Dublin Castle's Ship Street or Dame Street gates; the Dubh Linn Garden lawn just outside is a free place to sit when the museum is closed. The roof garden is only opened in dry weather.
spots.hours: approx 9:45am-5:30pm, Wed till 8pm, Sun from noon; closed Mon in winter (check site)

safety.note: Staffed public museum inside the Dublin Castle grounds.

spots.name: National Library of Ireland Reading Room
spots.blurb: The domed 1890 Reading Room on Kildare Street is one of the quietest big rooms in Dublin: green-shaded lamps, a ring of desks under the cupola, and nothing louder than a page turning. It is a working research library, but anyone can get a free reader's ticket at the front desk and sit with their own book or laptop.
spots.tips: Bring photo ID for the reader's ticket and leave bags in the lockers; Mon-Wed after 5pm is the calm window once students thin out. No food or drink inside.
spots.hours: Mon-Wed 9:30am-7:45pm, Thu-Fri to 4:45pm, Sat to 12:45pm (check site)

safety.note: Staffed national library with security at the door.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known institution; Wikipedia title kept on reviewer knowledge (not searched).

spots.name: Grand Canal at Portobello
spots.blurb: The stretch of the Grand Canal between Portobello Bridge and Baggot Street is a Dublin institution: lock gates, swans, a towpath lined with benches and the bronze Patrick Kavanagh sitting on his own bench near Mespil Road. On warm evenings much of the neighbourhood is on the bank with a coffee. Walk east for the calmer, tree-lined section.
spots.tips: The Portobello lock gets crowded and loud on hot evenings; the benches between Leeson Street and Baggot Street bridges are quieter. Bring something to sit on, the grass banks get damp.

safety.note: Towpath is lit and busy till late in summer; Portobello harbour can get rowdy and littered on warm nights, so head east of Leeson Street bridge for quiet and keep back from the unfenced water edge after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Public canal towpath; no specific Wikipedia article for this stretch, so title left null.

spots.name: Sandymount Strand
spots.blurb: A vast tidal beach on the south side of Dublin Bay where the sea retreats a long way at low tide and the Poolbeg chimneys stand in the middle of the view. Locals walk the promenade at all hours, sit on the wall by the Martello tower and watch the light change over Howth. Sunrise here is one of the best free shows in the city.
spots.tips: Take the DART to Sandymount and walk down to Strand Road; the promenade benches near the tower catch the morning sun. If you walk out on the sand, watch the tide, which comes in fast and has cut people off.

sources.title: Visit Sandymount Strand with Discover Ireland

safety.note: Promenade is lit and residential; stay off the sand flats after dark and never walk far out on an incoming tide.

spots.verifyNote: Wikipedia title confirmed from search result URL; tide hazard noted in the article, reflected in tips and note.

spots.name: Great South Wall to Poolbeg Lighthouse
spots.blurb: A roughly four-kilometre round-trip walk on a granite sea wall straight out into Dublin Bay, ending at the squat red Poolbeg Lighthouse. Out at the end you have the whole bay around you, ships sliding past close enough to wave at, and the city reduced to a line on the horizon. It is a classic Dublin place to clear your head at golden hour.
spots.tips: Drive or cycle to the small car park at the end of Pigeon House Road, then walk; there is no shelter so bring a windproof layer. Skip it in strong winds or high swell when waves break over the wall.

safety.note: The wall is unlit, unrailed and exposed; walk it in daylight or at sunset with time to get back before dark, and never in storms or high swell.

spots.verifyNote: Long-established public walk; Wikipedia title kept on reviewer knowledge (not searched). Kept at caution for exposure.

spots.name: Clontarf Promenade
spots.blurb: A flat, wide seafront path running from Fairview towards the Bull Wall along the north shore of Dublin Bay, with benches facing the water. It is where Clontarf goes to walk the dog, jog, or just sit and look at the Poolbeg chimneys and the mountains beyond. Lit along its length and used late into the evening.
spots.tips: Start near Clontarf Baths and head towards the wooden bridge for the widest views; the benches near the yacht club catch the sunrise. Bring a coat, the wind comes straight off the bay.

safety.note: Lit promenade beside a busy road and houses; joggers and walkers around until late.

spots.verifyNote: Public seafront path; no dedicated Wikipedia article, title left null.

spots.name: North Bull Island
spots.blurb: A five-kilometre sand island in Dublin Bay, reached by a wooden bridge or a causeway, with Dollymount Strand on the seaward side and salt marsh and dunes behind. Ten minutes' walk from the car park you are alone with the waders, the wind and a very big sky. On clear nights it is one of the darker places inside the city.
spots.tips: Cross via the causeway from James Larkin Road and walk north along the beach away from the kite-surfers; low tide leaves acres of firm sand. Bring layers, there is no shelter.

safety.note: Unlit and empty after dark; for stargazing stay near the causeway car park, go with a friend, and do not leave valuables in the car.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known nature reserve; Wikipedia title kept on reviewer knowledge (not searched).

spots.name: National Botanic Gardens
spots.blurb: Free botanic gardens on the River Tolka in Glasnevin, with restored Victorian glasshouses, a river walk, a rose garden and benches everywhere. It is calm on weekday mornings, and when the rain comes the Palm House and the Curvilinear Range let you sit among the tropical plants and wait it out. The cafe by the entrance is fine for a slow coffee.
spots.tips: Enter from Botanic Road; the quietest corners are the river walk and the arboretum at the far end. The glasshouses close a little before the gardens, so do those first.
spots.hours: approx 9am-5pm weekdays, 10am-6pm weekends in summer; to 4:30pm winter (check OPW site)
spots.verifyNote: Well-known national gardens; Wikipedia title kept on reviewer knowledge (not searched).

spots.name: Killiney Hill
spots.blurb: A wooded hill on the south edge of the city with an obelisk on top and a view that takes in Killiney Bay, Bray Head and the Wicklow Mountains, then the whole of Dublin Bay when you turn around. It is a twenty-minute climb from the car park or Killiney DART, and the summit rocks are a fine place to sit with a flask.
spots.tips: Park at the Killiney Hill car park off Killiney Hill Road or walk up from Dalkey village; the obelisk gets busy on Sunday afternoons, so go early or at golden hour. Paths are steep in places, wear proper shoes.

safety.note: Unlit after dark and some paths pass steep drops; leave the summit with enough light to get back to the car park or the road.

spots.name: Books Upstairs
spots.blurb: Dublin's oldest independent bookshop (since 1978), now in a Georgian building on D'Olier Street with a literary cafe on the first floor: armchairs, windows over the street and a strong Irish literature and poetry section downstairs. Buy a coffee and a book and stay a while; readings happen some evenings.
spots.tips: The window tables upstairs are the prize and it is quietest on weekday mornings. Check the events listing if you want a reading rather than silence.

sources.title: Books Upstairs | Dublin UNESCO City of Literature

safety.note: City-centre shop on a main street beside Trinity College.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed open at 17 D'Olier Street with first-floor cafe; no English Wikipedia article for the shop, so title set to null.

spots.name: St Kevin's Park, Camden Row
spots.blurb: A small walled council park inside the churchyard of a ruined 18th-century church (on a site first recorded in 1226), one turn off busy Camden Street and almost silent. Old gravestones lean along the walls, a few benches sit under the trees, and you can eat lunch here without seeing a single tourist.
spots.tips: The gate is on Camden Row beside the old church; it is locked at dusk. Bring a coffee from Camden Street, there is nothing inside but benches and trees.
spots.hours: approx 9am-dusk; check Dublin City Council site
